implementation_notes: abc.ABC (or a custom ABCMeta) plus @abstractmethod declares a contract whose subclasses cannot be instantiated until every abstract method is overridden: enforcement happens when the object is created, which is Python's substitute for a compile-time implementor check. The contract class itself holds no state - abstract methods carry docstrings or ellipsis bodies - and register()/__subclasshook__() let unrelated classes be treated as implementations, at the price of no method checking at all. Use it when you control the hierarchy and want a missing override to raise TypeError immediately; the structural alternative is typing.Protocol.
code_sketch:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):                 # contract: no instance state
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self) -> float: ...

class Square(Shape):              # state belongs to the implementation
    def __init__(self, side: float) -> None: self._side = side
    def area(self) -> float: return self._side ** 2

Square(2.0).area()   # 4.0 ;  Shape() raises TypeError
pitfalls: The check fires at instantiation, not at subclass definition: class Broken(Shape): pass imports cleanly and fails only when someone constructs it.
register() and __subclasshook__() insert types into the ABC hierarchy without checking that the methods exist, so isinstance-based satisfaction is claimed rather than verified.
Abstractness is only recomputed at class creation (update_abstractmethods() is needed otherwise), and adding an abstract method to a published ABC breaks third-party subclasses at instantiation time.

variants.name: typing.Protocol structural contract
variants.implementation_notes: A Protocol subclass declares the contract without creating an inheritance requirement: any object with matching members is assignable, and a static checker (mypy, pyright) verifies the shape, which is static duck typing rather than a nominal base class - the classic interface class is replaced by a type description that exists only for the checker. Add @runtime_checkable when isinstance must work, remembering that runtime protocol checks test member presence only, never signatures. Use it for implementations that are unrelated, come from other packages, or should not inherit from the ABC machinery.
variants.code_sketch:
from typing import Protocol

class Reader(Protocol):           # structural contract; no base class needed
    def read(self, n: int) -> bytes: ...

class SocketReader:               # satisfies Reader implicitly
    def read(self, n: int) -> bytes: return self._sock.recv(n)

def first_block(r: Reader) -> bytes: return r.read(4096)  # checked statically
pitfalls: Protocols are erased at run time: isinstance against a protocol raises TypeError unless it is @runtime_checkable, and even then only member presence is checked, not signatures or semantics.

A protocol can be subclassed explicitly without implementing it (an attribute set to None in the subclass satisfies the checker), and a non-protocol base downgrades the class to a regular ABC - both silently change what the contract means.
Structural assignability makes accidental matches cheap: an unrelated class with a similarly named member may be accepted, and protocols with non-method members cannot be used with issubclass.
